title: An Updated Agenda for America’s School Finance Reforms September 17, 2026 https://fordhaminstitute.org/national/commentary/updated-agenda-americas-school-finance-reforms
author: Aaron Garth Smith
source: Thomas B. Fordham Institute, Flypaper (fordhaminstitute.org), September 11, 2026,
summary: Aaron Garth Smith argues that K-12 finance reform, long organized around funding equity, needs a new agenda suited to an era of declining enrollment, mounting legacy costs, and falling achievement. He lays out the pressures: public school enrollment down 1.4 million since the pandemic with another 2.7 million projected, nearly $400 billion in teacher pension debt, non-teaching staff now more than half of all employees, and a decade-long learning recession despite large funding increases. His response is three policy goals with eight concrete reforms. For transparency and accountability, he proposes fiscal health frameworks like Texas's A-to-F district ratings, school capacity data, and rolling back local levies when enrollment falls. For sustainability, he calls for pension reform and funding based on current-year enrollment rather than 'ghost students.' For return on investment, he urges modernizing funding systems to work with ESAs and open enrollment, giving charter schools first access to vacant buildings, and deregulating class-size mandates, staffing ratios, and credential-based pay. The move of the piece is to shift the central question from how much is spent to how productively it is spent.
points: Smith argues the pre-pandemic pattern of large, sustained funding increases alongside stagnant results shows states cannot simply spend their way to better achievement.
Teacher pension debt of about $9,300 per student crowds out resources such as competitive salaries, and states owe those constitutionally protected obligations regardless of enrollment.
Funding 'ghost students' who are no longer enrolled, and local levies that do not fall with enrollment, remove districts' incentive to right-size by closing half-empty schools.
States should publish building utilization data and pair it with right-of-first-refusal and co-location laws so proven charter schools can use vacant or underused facilities.
Mandates like class-size limits, counselor staffing ratios, and pay tied to degrees limit local spending discretion and push districts toward hiring non-teaching staff.
quotes: But the latest research, along with mounting fiscal challenges for many school districts, underscores a need for fresh thinking in an era that’s no longer defined by savage inequalities.

Pension debt crowds out dollars available for things that drive results—like competitive salaries that would attract and retain the best teachers—and states are on the hook for their pension promises, which are constitutionally protected, regardless of how many students are in classrooms.
Pre-pandemic trends, including large and sustained K–12 funding increases, suggest that states can’t simply spend their way to better student achievement.

As a result, districts can end up collecting more money to serve fewer students and have less incentive to right-size. When enrollment declines hit a specified threshold, local tax rates should be rolled back to maintain an inflation-adjusted per-student amount.
This makes budgets more predictable, but it is also expensive and disincentivizes districts from right-sizing.

They also encourage or require districts to pay teachers based on educational attainment, which is weakly related to student achievement. These and other regulations, while well-intentioned, limit local spending discretion, incentivize hiring non-teaching staff, and ultimately prevent public schools from competing on a level playing field.
